Evermore
ĕv'ĕr-mōr
adv. (always, perpetually; in the Authorized Version chiefly for evermore, the settled unending state of a thing God has established)
From ever (Anglo-Saxon aefre) plus more — an intensified ever, as one might say ever and further. English built the compound to say more than ever alone could.

Biblical Definition

Evermore is not a mere synonym for always; in the Authorized Version it usually attaches to something God has settled and will not revisit. It fixes the throne: “I will settle him in mine house and in my kingdom for ever: and his throne shall be established for evermore” (1Ch 17:14) — the Davidic covenant, whose terms reach past Solomon to the Son of David whose kingdom has no end. It fixes the believer's portion: “in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore” (Psa 16:11) — a verse Peter preaches at Pentecost as a prophecy of the resurrection, so that the pleasures for evermore are secured by an empty tomb and not by an optimistic temperament. And Paul turns it into a command in the shortest verse of his letters: “Rejoice evermore” (1Th 5:16), which is only issuable as a command because the ground of the joy is outside the circumstances. The crowd at Capernaum uses it too, and wrongly: “Lord, evermore give us this bread” (Joh 6:34) — asking for a perpetual supply of loaves from the One who was offering them Himself.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines evermore as always, eternally, at all times, and notes the phrase for evermore as denoting an unending continuance.

expand to see more

EVERMORE, adv. Always; eternally; at all times.

He shall be blessed for evermore. Ps. xxxvii.

2. Continually; without intermission.

Note. Compounded of ever and more, an intensive form of ever.

Key Scripture

Psa 16:11 — "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore."

1Ch 17:14 — "But I will settle him in mine house and in my kingdom for ever: and his throne shall be established for evermore."

1Th 5:16 — "Rejoice evermore."

Joh 6:34 — "Then said they unto him, Lord, evermore give us this bread."

Modern Corruption

The unending state is emptied at both ends — annihilationism ends the punishment, and universalism ends the distinction — so that for evermore is left describing nothing in particular.

expand to see more

Scripture uses the same vocabulary of unending duration for the blessedness of the redeemed and the punishment of the unredeemed, and it uses it in the same sentence at Mat 25:46: “these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal”. Annihilationism, now common among evangelicals who find the doctrine intolerable, must break the parallel and read one everlasting as unending and the other as terminal. Universalism must break it the other way. Both proposals rest on what God's love would supposedly not allow rather than on what God has said, and both leave the believer's evermore resting on the same weakened word.

The doctrine is not cruelty; it is the seriousness of sin against an infinitely worthy God, and the LBCF holds it plainly. It is also what makes Psa 16:11 worth anything. Pleasures for evermore are only a comfort if evermore means what it says, and Peter's use of the psalm at Pentecost (Act 2:25-28) ties the promise to a fact in history — the flesh that did not see corruption. The command of 1Th 5:16 stands on the same ground: rejoice evermore, because the thing you rejoice in has been settled for evermore.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English ever + more; rendering Hebrew olam (H5769), the age or perpetuity, often with ad (H5703), and Greek pantote (G3842), always, or eis tous aionas, unto the ages.

expand to see more

Hebrew olam (H5769) — the hidden or unbounded time; “for ever” and “for evermore” both render it.

Hebrew ad olam — unto perpetuity; the phrase of 1Ch 17:14, of the Davidic throne.

Hebrew netsach (H5331) — enduring, everlasting; “pleasures for evermore” in Psa 16:11.

Greek pantote (G3842) — always, at all times; Paul's command chairete pantote, Rejoice evermore (1Th 5:16).

Greek eis ton aiona — unto the age; the Septuagint and New Testament rendering of olam, and the phrase Christ uses of the Comforter abiding “for ever” (Joh 14:16).

Usage

"“His throne shall be established for evermore” — the Davidic covenant, settled and not revisited."

"“Pleasures for evermore” — secured by resurrection, not by temperament."

"“Lord, evermore give us this bread” — asking a perpetual supply of loaves from the Bread Himself."
